body.text: From alien abductions to government cover-ups, conspiracy theories have long surrounded one of Australia's greatest aviation mysteries.
In August 1981, a light plane registered VH-MDX disappeared from radar over the Barrington Tops National Park on the NSW Mid North Coast.
Pilot Michael "Mike" Hutchins, 52, had been engaged to ferry home four passengers who had spent a week sailing a yacht north to Queensland for a friend.
More than four decades later, there is still no trace of the plane or those on board.
While evidence points to a conventional explanation for the crash, conspiracy theories have endured.
So, why do people turn to conspiracies, even when the evidence tells another story?
Rumours start early on
Glenn Cook still remembers hearing theories about what happened to the plane in the days after it disappeared.
"There were all sorts of rumours," he said.
The Newcastle man was working as a camera operator for a local news station when VH-MDX went down.

From his news helicopter, he joined scores of police, NSW State Emergency Service volunteers, forestry workers, army personnel, media, and bushwalkers scouring the area for wreckage in a nine-day search for the aircraft.
But when no trace of the plane was found, conspiracies took hold, helped by speculation about Mr Price, a New South Wales police inspector.
"Local radio stations were starting to throw theories around," Mr Cook said.
"The biggest one was that the mob or some criminal gang had blown the plane up with something to do with the policeman," Mr Cook said.
"I've heard people think the aliens took them."
'Conspiracies avoid discomfort'
Investigators say the most likely scenario is that the plane suffered mechanical issues after hitting bad weather, the pilot became disorientated, then crashed.
As for not finding the plane? They say it's highly likely the densely forested terrain of the Barrington Tops has so far made locating the wreckage impossible.
Regardless, the theories that surfaced in the days after the crash have endured.

Kate FitzGerald, who is a PhD candidate at Queensland University of Technology researching conspiracy theories, said many people tended to believe in them for a sense of safety and security, especially when there was a mystery or unanswered questions.
"A lack of information can cause stress and anxiety," Ms FitzGerald said.
"Conspiracy theories can fill that [gap] … and help us make sense of the world around us by looking at patterns and creating connections."
Ms FitzGerald said social psychologists had also found the human brain thrived on knowledge and being "certain" about something.

"Even if that belief comes from a flawed source of knowledge and is not necessarily backed up by evidence, human brains are still happier having that belief rather than things being left as a mystery," she said.
Conspiracies and social climate
While many of the theories surrounding VH-MDX are outright outlandish, others are rooted in real-world events and legitimate public distrust.
Ms FitzGerald said it was important to consider the social climate at the time of any given conspiracy theory.
One of the most prevalent conspiracies surrounding VH-MDX's disappearance is centred around the fact a police officer was on board the aircraft.

Despite zero supporting evidence, theories surfaced that the passenger, NSW Police Inspector Ken Price, was part of a police-aligned criminal enterprise smuggling gold, drugs or money and that after the crash, authorities covered the evidence.
"At the time in New South Wales, community members had been dealing with what was actually very real corruption from the New South Wales police force," Ms FitzGerald said.
This was revealed in the Wood Royal Commission in 1997, which found corruption, bribery, and drug-dealing was widespread within the NSW Police force in the force in the 70s and 80s.

"While I'm not condoning or supporting this theory, it's not entirely surprising that the public had lost trust in the police force and their ability to provide an accurate and official narrative of the events,"
Ms FitzGerald said.
"It's a pattern that we very much see with conspiracy theorists, where they take pieces of evidence often out of context and sort of bring them together to create a new cohesive sort of narrative."
The wider impact of conspiracies
Ken Price's daughter, Merrilea Price, was 23 when her father went missing.
"It was dreadful … I couldn't believe it," she said.
Ms Price said she was her "daddy's little girl" and hearing the rumours about her father was upsetting.
"Dad loved his job … he took it really seriously," she said.
"He wasn't a corrupt cop."
Ms FitzGerald said conspiracies could be damaging to the people they were centred on.
"People need to be so careful, because in the case of VH-MDX, these are real, everyday people who tragically lost their lives in a very scary accident," she said.
"And there's never been closure for those families."
